newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing starts end 2-month slide in November.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing starts end 2-month slide in November.

text.p: U.S. housing starts ended a two-month slide with a surprisingly strong recovery in November, hinting lower mortgage rates may have sparked an uptrend, economists said on Tuesday.

Housing starts beat Wall Street expectations for a mild rebound, jumping 9.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.514 million units in November -- the biggest gain since July 1995. October starts were revised upward to 1.386 million units. A Reuter poll of economists had called for an average 1.390 million unit annual rate in November.

"You're seeing a quick reaction to the recent rally in the U.S. Treasury market by builders in general. They feel rates will remain on the friendly side, and starts and permits benefited from this," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Rising Treasury prices mean falling yields since the two are inversely related. Lower yields usually act as a precursor to lower mortgage rates, which encourage the sale of homes and construction, economists said.
Changes in housing starts tend to lag changes in mortgage rates, so a rise in rates seen in the first half of the year was partially responsible for the October-September slide.
Conversely, a drop in rates in the second half is expected to continue to aid the housing sector in the coming months.

"We have seen mortgage rates move down a bit over the past couple of months and (the November rise in starts) is the followthrough. I think we can expect to see some decent looking numbers for the next couple of months," said Christopher Low, economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Housing should provide some, but limited, support to U.S. economic growth going into the new year, economists said.
"As you move forward in the months to come, housing should continue to provide some support," Flanagan said.
While Low said November's increase in housing construction encouraged economic expansion, he does not see the housing sector adding greatly to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth.
"It should be helping the economy, but as far as contributions to GDP, I think we will see flat numbers because it's housing over a long period of time that impacts GDP growth," Low said.

Economists said the revival in November housing starts was likely expected by Federal Reserve economists given the recent decline in bond yields and their expectations for a fall in starts in previous months.
"Months ago, Fed Chairman (Alan) Greenspan and others were looking for some pullback given the hike in rates over the summer and the opposite has been true recently," Flanagan said.
U.S. Treasuries fell sharply, most significantly in the longer maturities, after the housing data were released.

The benchmark 30-year long bond dropped 17/32 in a knee-jerk reaction. At 0930 EST/1430 GMT, the benchmark was off 27/32 at 97-16/32 to yield 6.69 pecent as the sell-off gained momentum following a 0.7 percent rise in the weekly BTM/Schroder chain store sales index.
